results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. When a phased-out permanent phases in, it does not trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities. Phasing in does not cause a permanent to change zones; the game simply treats it as though it exists again. Because enters-the-battlefield triggers are zone-change triggers that fire only when a permanent actually moves from another zone onto the battlefield, and phasing in is not a zone change, those abilities do not trigger.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, its controller only needs to assign 1 damage to each creature blocking it before trampling over the rest. Deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of combat damage count as lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage (rule 702.2c). Trample then allows the attacking creature's controller to assign excess damage to the defending player or planeswalker once all blockers have been assigned lethal damage (rule 702.19b). Because 1 damage from a deathtouch source is lethal, the attacker can assign exactly 1 damage to each blocker and the remainder to the defending player or planeswalker. This interaction is also reflected in the excess damage rules: any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess if the source has deathtouch (rule 120.4a). If there are no blockers when damage is assigned, trample already sends all damage to the defending player/planeswalker (rule 702.19d), so deathtouch doesn't change that scenario.

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes, storm is a triggered ability that can be countered. Storm is defined as a triggered ability that functions on the stack [702.40a]. Triggered abilities on the stack are not spells, so they can't be countered by effects that counter only spells, but they can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities [113.9]. Therefore, a storm ability can be countered by an effect like "counter target ability," but not by a typical "counter target spell" effect.

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text:
No, you cannot. A card with a hybrid mana symbol has a color identity that includes all colors in that symbol. For example, a card with a {R/G} hybrid symbol has a color identity of both red and green. Under Commander deck construction rules, every color in a card's color identity must be present in your commander's color identity. If your commander's color identity is only red, then a card with a {R/G} symbol includes green, which is not in your commander's identity, so the card is illegal.

Rule 903.5c states that a card can be included only if every color in its color identity is also found in the commander's color identity. Rule 903.4f defines color identity as the colors of any mana symbols in the card's mana cost or rules text. Rule 107.4e clarifies that a hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors. Thus, a hybrid symbol like {R/G} contributes both red and green to the card's color identity. If your commander lacks one of those colors, the card cannot be included.

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so you cannot cast spells or activate abilities. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held and put onto the stack at the beginning of the upkeep step, before the active player gets priority.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. They remain attacking creatures until they are removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. The end of combat step is part of the combat phase, so the combat phase has not yet ended. Creatures are only removed from combat as the end of combat step ends (rule 511.3). Therefore, throughout the entire end of combat step, attacking creatures retain their attacking status unless some other effect has already removed them from combat.

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Lands are never cast as spells. Instead, you **play** a land as a special action. Playing a land doesn't use the stack, can't be countered, and doesn't count as casting a spell. This applies even to cards that have both the land type and another card type (like artifact lands) — they can only be played as lands, never cast. Lands have no mana cost, and you don't pay any costs to play them; you simply put them onto the battlefield from your hand during your main phase when the stack is empty and you have priority, provided you haven't already played a land that turn (unless an effect allows otherwise).

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: Yes, you can sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves. When a creature enters the battlefield and its evoke cost was paid, the evoke triggered ability goes on the stack. While that ability is on the stack, you can respond to it by activating an ability or casting a spell that sacrifices the creature. The evoke triggered ability does not require the creature to still be on the battlefield when it resolves — it only checks whether the evoke cost was paid when the creature entered. If the creature is sacrificed in response, the evoke ability will still resolve and instruct its controller to sacrifice it, but since the creature is already gone, that part of the instruction simply does nothing. This is because the evoke ability is not a cost that must be paid; it is a triggered ability that creates a one-shot effect upon resolution, and sacrificing the creature is part of that effect, not a condition for the ability to trigger or resolve.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, losing all abilities includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are a type of ability (rule 702.1 defines them as a shorthand for common abilities, and rule 702.1d confirms that referring to an object "with [keyword ability]" means the same as "with a [keyword ability] ability"). An effect that says a permanent "loses all abilities" removes every ability it has, including all keyword abilities, whether printed on the card or granted by another effect. Rule 113.10b states that an effect which removes an ability removes all instances of it. Rule 603.6b provides a direct example: if an effect reads "All creatures lose all abilities," a creature's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability (which could be a keyword ability) is lost the moment it enters, so that ability won't trigger.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you are already at your maximum hand size. The maximum hand size rule only forces you to discard down to that number during your cleanup step [514.1][402.2]. It does not prevent you from drawing cards or having more cards in your hand at other times. If you draw cards and end up with more than your maximum hand size, you will simply have to discard the excess during your next cleanup step.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker has zero loyalty counters, its loyalty is 0, and it is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. There is no such thing as negative loyalty counters; if an effect (like damage) would remove more counters than the planeswalker has, it simply removes all of them, leaving the planeswalker with 0 loyalty, which then causes it to die. This is governed by the state-based action that checks for a planeswalker with loyalty 0 [704.5i, 306.9]. Loyalty is defined as the number of loyalty counters on the planeswalker [306.5c], and counters themselves are markers that can only be placed or removed—they don't go negative [122.1e]. So "0 or less loyalty counters" effectively means the planeswalker has no counters, loyalty is 0, and it dies immediately before any player receives priority.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No, non-creature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" is defined as "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" and applies only to creatures and planeswalkers. A non-creature artifact is neither a creature nor a planeswalker, so moving from the battlefield to the graveyard is not a "death" event for it. This is stated directly in the glossary entry for "Dies" and in rule 700.4.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: You lose the game the next time state-based actions are checked. When you are required to draw a card from an empty library, you attempt to draw but there are no cards to draw. This attempt triggers a state-based action: the next time a player would receive priority (which is right after the current spell or ability finishes resolving, or during the draw step), the game sees that you attempted to draw from an empty library and you lose. This is true whether you need to draw one card or many—you draw as many as possible (zero) and then lose. If the draw is optional (e.g., “you may draw a card”), you can still choose to draw and then lose, but if you decline, you don’t attempt to draw and don’t lose from this rule.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps, in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. (If no attackers are declared, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped [506.1]. If any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps [506.1].)

As the defending player, you receive priority during each of these steps after the active player has had priority and passed, except that turn-based actions happen first and don't use the stack. Specifically:

- **Beginning of combat step**: After any turn-based action (in multiplayer games where opponents don't automatically become defending players, the active player chooses a defending player [703.4h]), the active player gets priority. Once the active player passes, you (the defending player) get priority. This is confirmed by the shortcut example where the nonactive player (defending player) holds priority during the beginning of combat step [732.2b].
- **Declare attackers step**: The active player declares attackers as a turn-based action (not detailed in the provided rules, but implied by the structure). Then the active player gets priority, and after they pass, you get priority.
- **Declare blockers step**: You declare blockers as a turn-based action immediately after the step begins [703.4j][509.1]. Then the active player gets priority, and after they pass, you get priority.
- **Combat damage step**: Combat damage is assigned (in APNAP order) and then dealt simultaneously as turn-based actions [703.4k][510.1][510.2]. No player can cast spells or activate abilities between assignment and dealing [510.2]. After damage is dealt, the active player gets priority, and after they pass, you get priority.
- **End of combat step**: No turn-based actions occur. The active player gets priority once the step begins [511.1]. After they pass, you get priority.

In a two-player game, you are the nonactive player and thus the defending player [506.2]. In multiplayer games using the attack multiple players option, all opponents are defending players [802.2], and you would receive priority in turn order after the active player passes. The priority system itself is governed by rule 117.1, though the exact sequence of priority after each step's turn-based actions is not fully spelled out in the provided rules; the above is inferred from the given examples and turn-based action rules.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities don't use the stack, so they can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. They resolve immediately after being activated or triggered. This applies to both activated mana abilities (rule 605.3b) and triggered mana abilities (rule 605.4a). Rule 405.6c also confirms that mana abilities resolve immediately. If an ability produces mana but has a target or triggers from something other than a mana ability, it is not a mana ability (rule 605.5a) and can be responded to normally.

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: Based on the provided rules, it cannot be determined whether a player can respond to a cost being paid. The rules given define costs and how they are paid in various contexts (e.g., during declaring attackers or blockers, or as part of optional costs), but they do not include the comprehensive rules for casting spells (rule 601.2) or any explicit statement that paying a cost does not use the stack and cannot be responded to. While the rules for declaring attackers and blockers indicate that paying costs during those turn-based actions does not use the stack, this does not generalize to all cost payments. Without the missing rules, a definitive answer is not possible.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are a system that determines the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object's characteristics. The game starts with the object's printed values (or the values defined by the effect that created a token or copy), then applies all applicable continuous effects in a fixed sequence of layers. Within each layer or sublayer, effects are normally applied in timestamp order (earlier timestamp first), but a dependency can override that order. The application is continuous and automatic; any change to an object's characteristics is instantaneous.

The layers, in order, are:
- Layer 1: Rules and effects that modify copiable values (including copy effects and merge effects).
- Layer 2: Control-changing effects.
- Layer 3: Text-changing effects.
- Layer 4: Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype).
- Layer 5: Color-changing effects.
- Layer 6: Ability-adding effects.
- Layer 7: Power- and toughness-changing effects. Layer 7 has sublayers; the provided rules mention sublayer 7b (effects that set power and toughness to a specific value) and sublayer 7c (effects that modify power and toughness without setting them).

If an effect has parts that apply in different layers, each part is applied in its appropriate layer, and the effect continues to apply to the same set of objects even if the ability generating it is removed during the process.

Example (from rule 613.5): A 2/2 creature (Gray Ogre) gets a +1/+1 counter (layer 7c, making it 3/3), then a spell gives it +4/+4 until end of turn (layer 7c, making it 7/7), then an enchantment gives creatures you control +0/+2 (layer 7c, making it 7/9), then an effect makes it become 0/1 until end of turn (layer 7b, setting base to 0/1). The final result is 5/8 (0/1 base, plus +4/+4, +0/+2, and +1/+1 from the counter).

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action: if a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name, that player chooses one to keep and puts the rest into their owners' graveyards. This applies only to legendary permanents (creatures, planeswalkers, artifacts, enchantments, lands, etc.) that share a name and are controlled by the same player. It does not apply to legendary instants or sorceries; those have a casting restriction instead (you can't cast them unless you control a legendary creature or planeswalker). The old planeswalker uniqueness rule has been removed, and all planeswalkers now have the legendary supertype, so they follow the same legend rule. Legendary tokens are created with a name and are subject to the rule just like nontoken permanents.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Your creature dies the next time state-based actions are checked after the lethal damage is marked on it. This happens automatically just before any player would receive priority.

Damage being marked on a creature (e.g., from a spell like Lightning Bolt or from combat) does not itself destroy the creature [120.5]. Instead, the game rules check for lethal damage as a state-based action [704.5g]. State-based actions are performed each time a player would get priority, and they are repeated until no more such actions apply [117.5, 117.2d]. So after the damage is marked, the next time a player would receive priority—for example, after a spell or ability resolves, or after combat damage is dealt—the game checks state-based actions, sees that the creature has damage marked on it greater than or equal to its toughness, and destroys it. This all happens without using the stack and before any player can respond.

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: No, you cannot cast your commander from exile simply because it is your commander. The Commander rules only grant permission to cast a commander from the command zone. Rule [903.8] states: "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone." It does not provide any permission to cast a commander from exile. To cast any spell from exile, you need a specific rule or effect that allows it, as required by rule [601.3f]. Without such an effect (for example, if the commander has plot or you control an effect that lets you cast spells from exile), you cannot cast your commander from exile. If your commander is in exile, you may instead use the state-based action from rule [903.9a] to put it into the command zone, from which you can then cast it.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text: During the cleanup step, two turn-based actions happen in order. First, if the active player's hand size exceeds their maximum (normally seven), they discard down to that number [514.1]. Second, all damage is removed from permanents and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end simultaneously [514.2] [703.4p]. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast or abilities activated [514.3]. However, if any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting (including those that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"), those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put on the stack, and the active player gets priority [514.3a] [704.3]. Players may then cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins [514.3a]. If no state-based actions or triggered abilities are waiting, the step ends without any player getting priority [500.3] [704.3]. Additionally, if an effect ends the turn during the cleanup step, a new cleanup step begins [724.1d].

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked each time a player would receive priority, and also during the cleanup step. Specifically, the game performs a check right before any player gets priority, and it repeats that check until no more state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack [704.3, 117.5]. During the cleanup step, if any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting, those state-based actions are performed, then triggered abilities go on the stack, and the active player gets priority; otherwise, no player gets priority and the step ends [514.3a]. State-based actions are not checked during the resolution of a spell or ability—only after that resolution is complete and a player would next receive priority [704.4].

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: You can concede a game at any time. Conceding doesn't use the stack, happens immediately, and causes you to leave the game and lose it. This right cannot be overridden by any card effect or by another player controlling your turn.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is the player whose turn it is. This is stated directly in rule 102.1 and the glossary entry for "Active Player." All other players are nonactive players. In a game using the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is, but the active player is still the individual player on that team whose turn it is (or, if the team's turn is taken collectively, the concept of a single active player may be modified by team rules). In standard play, simply look at whose turn is currently in progress.

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The player who cast the spell gets priority first. Rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Since a non-active player must have had priority to cast the spell, they regain priority immediately after casting it.

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The active player gets priority first after casting a spell. Rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Since the active player normally has priority when they cast a spell, they will be the first to receive priority again once the spell is on the stack.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes, you can hold priority to cast more spells after you've cast one. When you cast a spell while you have priority, you receive priority again immediately after the spell is cast (rule 117.3c, 601.2i). That means you can cast another spell right away without passing priority to your opponent(s). You can repeat this to cast multiple spells in succession, as long as each spell is legal to cast at that moment (for example, instants or spells with flash, since the stack is not empty). This is commonly referred to as "holding priority."

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Lore counters are put on Sagas in two distinct ways: as a replacement effect when the Saga enters the battlefield, and as a turn-based action at the beginning of each of its controller's precombat main phases.

1. **Entering the battlefield**: A Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter on it ([714.3a]). A Saga with read ahead enters with a number of lore counters chosen by its controller between one and its final chapter number ([714.3b], [702.155b]). Both are replacement effects that modify how the permanent enters; they don't use the stack.

2. **Precombat main phase**: Immediately after a player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities ([703.4f], [714.3c], [505.4]). This turn-based action doesn't use the stack and happens before any player receives priority in that phase.

Note that the turn-based action applies only to Sagas with chapter abilities (i.e., those that haven't been fully sacrificed yet). The state-based action that sacrifices a Saga when its lore counters reach or exceed its final chapter number ([714.4], [704.5s]) is checked separately after the lore counter is placed.

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is a triggered ability created by an effect that instructs a player to do something later in the game, rather than immediately when the spell or ability resolves. It always contains the word "when," "whenever," or "at," though that word usually doesn't begin the ability. Delayed triggered abilities are created during the resolution of spells or abilities, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as a result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action. They trigger only once—the next time their trigger event occurs—unless they have a stated duration like "this turn."

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities. Specifically, any text on an instant or sorcery spell is a spell ability unless it's an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the criteria in rule 113.6. These abilities function only while the spell is on the stack. This is because an ability is a characteristic an object can have (rule 113.1a), and a spell on the stack is an object. The rules explicitly define spell abilities as the instructions followed while an instant or sorcery spell resolves (rule 113.3a, "Spell Ability" definition).

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second explicitly allows players to activate mana abilities (and take special actions) even though it prevents casting other spells or activating non-mana abilities. This is stated directly in the split second rules: "As long as this spell is on the stack, players can’t cast other spells or activate abilities that aren’t mana abilities" [702.61a], and "Players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack" [702.61b]. Mana abilities themselves don't use the stack and can be activated at times when you normally couldn't activate other abilities, including while a split second spell is on the stack.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first, and Divination does not resolve.

When all players pass in succession, the top object on the stack resolves (rules 405.5, 117.4). Counterspell is on top of the stack targeting Divination, so Counterspell resolves first. As Counterspell resolves, its effect counters Divination (rule 701.6a). A countered spell is removed from the stack and put into its owner's graveyard; it doesn't resolve and none of its effects occur. Therefore, Divination is countered and never resolves.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign lethal damage equal to Vampire Nighthawk's toughness, which is 3. Since Charging Rhino is a 4/4 with trample, you assign 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk and the remaining 1 damage to the defending player. The deathtouch ability on Vampire Nighthawk does not change this because the rule that makes any nonzero damage lethal applies only when the source dealing the damage has deathtouch (rule 702.2c). Charging Rhino does not have deathtouch, so lethal damage is determined solely by the blocker's toughness (rule 302.4b, 702.19b).

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers when you cast the cascaded spell, and that triggered ability resolves **before** the cascaded spell resolves.

Here's why: When Shardless Agent's cascade ability resolves, you may cast the exiled noncreature spell without paying its mana cost. Casting that spell during the resolution of cascade puts it on the stack above the cascade ability (Shardless Agent ruling #1). The moment the spell becomes cast, prowess triggers (rule 601.2i). Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2 explicitly states: "Prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger. It will resolve before that spell." So after the cascade ability finishes resolving, the prowess triggered ability is put onto the stack above the cascaded spell, and it will resolve first, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 before the cascaded spell takes effect.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: Yes, state-based actions destroy the Grizzly Bears before Lightning Bolt resolves. The Grizzly Bears already has 2 damage marked on it, which equals its toughness of 2, so it has been dealt lethal damage. State-based actions are checked every time a player would receive priority, and they happen before that player actually gets priority. After Lightning Bolt is cast, the active player would receive priority, but first the game performs state-based actions. At that moment, the Grizzly Bears has lethal damage marked, so it is destroyed and put into its owner's graveyard. This all occurs while Lightning Bolt is still on the stack, before it resolves. (Lightning Bolt will then be countered on resolution for having no legal target, but that is a separate consequence.)

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Both triggers trigger at the beginning of your upkeep, before any player gets priority. The order they go on the stack is determined by APNAP order: you (the active player) put your Phyrexian Arena trigger on the stack first, then your opponent puts their trigger on top. So the opponent's trigger will resolve first. You do not get to choose the order.

When the upkeep step begins, all abilities that trigger "at the beginning of" that step trigger automatically (rule 500.6, 603.2b). Since the upkeep has no turn-based actions (503.1a), the next thing that happens is that those triggered abilities are put on the stack before the active player receives priority (117.3a). Because multiple abilities triggered since the last time a player received priority, they are placed on the stack in APNAP order (603.3b, 101.4). The active player puts each triggered ability they control on the stack in any order they choose, then the nonactive player does the same. Thus, your Phyrexian Arena trigger goes on the stack first, and your opponent's trigger goes on top of it. The opponent's trigger will therefore resolve first when players begin passing priority.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
Only the original sorcery card ends up in your hand. The copy created by Fork does not return a card to your hand.

When the original sorcery spell resolves, its buyback ability (rule 702.27a) replaces the normal graveyard destination with returning the card to its owner's hand, because you paid the buyback cost. Fork creates a copy of that spell on the stack (rule 707.10). That copy is not cast (Fork ruling #9) and has no physical card associated with it (Fork ruling #10). Fork ruling #8 explicitly states that if you copy a spell for which buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you. Therefore, the copy simply ceases to exist after it resolves, and no card is returned to your hand from it.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No token is created. Mimic Vat ruling #0 explicitly states that if the exiled card is a nonpermanent card (like the instant Lightning Bolt that was manifested), you can't create a token that's a copy of it, and no token is created. The ability resolves but produces no token.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both exiled creatures return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Fiend Hunter's two abilities are linked: the enters-the-battlefield ability that exiles a creature and the leaves-the-battlefield ability that returns "the exiled card" (rule 607.2a). Lithoform Engine's ruling #4 explicitly states that when you copy a linked ability, the copy is also linked to the second ability. The second ability then refers to all cards exiled by both the original ability and the copy. The ruling even uses Fiend Hunter as the example: "if Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability is copied and two creatures are exiled, they both return when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield." So both creatures you exiled will come back.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. Banishing Light's exile effect lasts "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield." Phasing out does not cause a permanent to leave the battlefield (rule 702.26d); it merely treats the permanent as though it doesn't exist while phased out. Because Banishing Light never actually left the battlefield, the condition for returning the exiled creature is not met. Additionally, Teferi's Protection ruling #21 explicitly states that one-shot effects waiting for a permanent to leave the battlefield (like Banishing Light's) won't happen when that permanent phases out. The creature remains in exile.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text: Yes, your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell while Emrakul is on the stack. Protection from instants is an ability that functions only while Emrakul is on the battlefield, not while it's a spell on the stack. If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the cast trigger ("When you cast this spell...") is a separate object on the stack and will still resolve. You will still gain control of the targeted opponent during their next turn, and they will take an extra turn after that.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes, Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit (assuming the cascade spell's mana value is 3 or greater). No, you cannot cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side for free unless the cascade spell's mana value is 8 or greater.

Cascade (rule 702.85a) exiles cards until you hit a nonland card with mana value less than the cascade spell's mana value. While in your library (a hidden zone), a double-faced card has only the characteristics of its front face, so Valki, God of Lies has mana value 2. If the cascade spell's mana value is 3 or more, Valki qualifies as a legal hit.

Once exiled, cascade allows you to cast that card without paying its mana cost, but only if the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value. For a modal double-faced card, you may choose which face to cast (Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16). However, Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor has mana value 7, so you can only cast it for free if the cascade spell's mana value is 8 or greater. If the cascade spell's mana value is 7 or less, you may still cast Valki, God of Lies (mana value 2) for free, but not Tibalt.

(If the cascade spell's mana value were 2 or less, Valki would not be a legal hit at all, but the question implies it was exiled, so we assume the cascade spell's mana value is at least 3.)
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #14

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You control one opponent's next turn (the one from the last trigger to resolve, assuming both triggers targeted the same opponent). You do get a second Emrakul—a token copy. Copying the Emrakul spell does **not** give you another control-a-turn trigger because the copy wasn't cast.

Here's why:

1. **Copying the cast trigger** – You used Lithoform Engine's first ability to copy Emrakul, the Promised End's triggered ability. The copy has the same source as the original (Lithoform Engine ruling #0) and you may choose new targets. Both the original and the copy will resolve, each trying to control the targeted opponent's next turn and give them an extra turn after that turn. If both target the same opponent, the last one to resolve overwrites the earlier one for the control effect (Emrakul ruling #14). However, each ability still creates an extra turn (Emrakul ruling #14), so that opponent will take two extra turns after the turn you control.

2. **Copying the Emrakul spell** – You then untapped Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key and used its third ability to copy the Emrakul permanent spell on the stack. The copy is put onto the stack and, as it resolves, becomes a token with the characteristics of Emrakul, the Promised End (rule 111.13). This gives you a second Emrakul (a token).

3. **No extra cast trigger** – The copy of the spell was not cast (rule 707.10; Lithoform Engine ruling #6). Emrakul's control-a-turn ability triggers only when you **cast** the spell, so copying it on the stack does not cause that ability to trigger again. You get no additional control effect from the token copy.

(Note: Because Emrakul is legendary, you'll have to choose one to keep when the token enters; the other will go to the graveyard as a state-based action.)

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text: Yes, you get two tokens. When you copy Mimic Vat's activated ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is put onto the stack and has the same source as the original ability—the same Mimic Vat (Lithoform Engine ruling #0; rule 707.10b). Both the original and the copy refer to "a card exiled with this artifact," which is a linked ability phrase that points to the card exiled by Mimic Vat's triggered ability (rule 607.3). As each ability resolves, it creates a token that's a copy of whatever card is currently exiled with Mimic Vat (Mimic Vat ruling #4). Since the same card remains exiled, both abilities create a token copy of that card. Each token gains haste and will be exiled at the beginning of the next end step.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, the total cost is {1}{G}{G} and you create zero 1/1 tokens. For the best value, you should choose X=2; then you pay {1}{G}{G} and create two 1/1 tokens.

Here's why. When you cast Awaken the Woods, you first announce the value of X (rule 107.3a). The mana cost is {X}{G}{G}. You have a permanent that makes your green spells cost {1} less; this reduction applies only to the generic mana portion of the cost. Then you determine the total cost (rule 601.2f): start with the mana cost, apply cost increases (none here), then cost reductions (the {1} reduction), and finally apply Trinisphere's effect if the mana component is less than three mana (Trinisphere ruling #0).

- With X=0, the mana cost is {G}{G}. The {1} reduction can't reduce colored mana, so the cost stays {G}{G} (2 mana). Trinisphere sees a spell that would cost less than three mana, so it forces the cost to three mana: you must pay an additional {1}, making the total {1}{G}{G}. X is 0, so you get no tokens.
- With X=1, the mana cost is {1}{G}{G} (3 mana). After the {1} reduction, the generic part becomes {0}, leaving {G}{G} (2 mana). Trinisphere again raises it to three mana, so you pay {1}{G}{G} and get one token.
- With X=2, the mana cost is {2}{G}{G} (4 mana). After the {1} reduction, the generic part is {1}, so the cost is {1}{G}{G} (3 mana). That's exactly three mana, so Trinisphere does nothing (it only applies if the cost is *less* than three). You pay {1}{G}{G} and get two tokens.
- With X=3, the cost after reduction is {2}{G}{G} (4 mana), no Trinisphere, so you pay {2}{G}{G} for three tokens.

Thus X=2 gives you the most tokens for the least mana while Trinisphere is on the battlefield.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead while Grist, the Hunger Tide is in your graveyard, because in that zone Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card (a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect). When Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability resolves, it returns Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control. However, once on the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide is no longer a creature—it is only a planeswalker. Animate Dead can only enchant a creature, so it cannot legally remain attached to Grist, the Hunger Tide. As a state-based action, Animate Dead is put into its owner's graveyard. This causes Animate Dead's delayed triggered ability to trigger, and when that trigger resolves, you must sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide. The net result is that Grist, the Hunger Tide briefly enters the battlefield and then is sacrificed.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps the four +1/+1 counters. No, Doubling Season does not double them.

Skullbriar's own ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." When it dies, it goes to the graveyard (not hand or library), so the counters stay. Then, as a commander, you may use the state-based action from rule 903.9a to put it into the command zone instead of the graveyard; that move is also to a zone that isn't hand or library, so the counters remain. When you later cast Skullbriar, it moves from the command zone to the stack and then to the battlefield — again, none of those zones are hand or library, so the counters stay on it the whole time. It enters the battlefield already carrying those four +1/+1 counters.

Doubling Season's second ability only applies when "an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control." The counters on Skullbriar are not being placed by an effect; they are simply retained as the card changes zones. As stated in Skullbriar's rulings, "The counters that remain on Skullbriar as it changes zones aren't 'placed' on Skullbriar. Effects like Doubling Season's ... won't affect those counters." Therefore, Doubling Season does not double them.
citations: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card text

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text:
No, you do not lose the game during that extra turn. However, the "lose the game" ability from Final Fortune doesn't simply vanish—it will trigger at the beginning of the next turn's end step instead.

When you activate Sundial of the Infinite before the end step, the turn ends immediately and the end step is skipped (rule 724.1d). According to Sundial of the Infinite's ruling #1, any "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities won't trigger that turn because the end step is skipped; they will trigger at the beginning of the end step of the next turn. Final Fortune's delayed trigger is exactly such an ability, so it waits for the next end step that actually occurs. This is different from skipping the extra turn entirely—Final Fortune's ruling #1 says you don't lose if you skip the extra turn, but here you are taking the extra turn and merely skipping its end step, so the trigger is postponed, not prevented.

Thus, you will lose the game at the beginning of the next turn's end step (likely your opponent's end step, or your own next turn's end step if you take another extra turn) unless you can avoid that trigger as well.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, after the Clone spell resolves and before any enters-the-battlefield triggers are put on the stack. Your opponent cannot respond to that choice itself. They can respond to the Clone spell while it's on the stack (before it resolves and you make the choice), or to any triggered abilities that result from Clone entering the battlefield, but the choice of what to copy is made without using the stack and cannot be responded to.

Clone's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how Clone enters the battlefield. According to rule 707.5, an object that enters "as a copy" becomes a copy as it enters, not after. The choice of which creature to copy is made as part of applying that replacement effect. The ability doesn't target (Clone ruling #0), so you simply choose a creature on the battlefield. No player gets priority during this process, so your opponent can't respond to the choice. Once Clone enters as a copy, any enters-the-battlefield abilities it gains will trigger and go on the stack, at which point players can respond normally.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total. The original Flooded Strand ability resolves, and the two copies created by Gogo, Master of Mimicry also resolve, each allowing you to search for a Plains or Island and put it onto the battlefield.

When you activate Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability with X=2 targeting the Flooded Strand ability on the stack, you put two copies of that ability onto the stack (Gogo ruling #6). A copy of an ability copies all decisions made for the original, including the fact that its costs were already paid, and has the same source as the original (707.10b; Gogo ruling #9). The copies are not activated, so they don't require you to pay the costs again. The original Flooded Strand was sacrificed as part of its cost, but the copies still resolve independently, each giving you a search. Therefore, you get one land from the original ability and one from each of the two copies, for a total of three lands.
